purpose_of_this_fixture: Tests a strong, hour-long discovery call with the PMO of a 400-person healthcare construction and renovation firm, delivered as a WebVTT transcript with '<v Speaker Name>' voice tags, where the account tier is stated plainly and therefore the Enterprise portfolio default fires. The plugin should: (1) Read 'We're on the enterprise plan, work management, about two hundred and twenty seats.' as the trigger for amendment A6 and include a portfolio with connected projects BY DEFAULT, recording the reason. This is the first fixture in the set where that default actually applies, and the client's own stated need agrees with it: a portfolio view across roughly forty active projects showing health, budget burn and the next owner milestone. It must be built with monday's portfolio and project tools, not plain boards dressed up as projects, with the projects connected and the roll-ups checked after creation. (2) Not quietly decide the portfolio's shape. The client uses 'portfolio' for the whole book of active work and 'program' for one health system's work under a master agreement ('A program is one health system's work under a master agreement.'), a job sits in both at once, and Cumberland's vice president of facilities wants the program as one thing. Whether that is one portfolio with a program grouping, or a portfolio per program, is a question for the consultant and the client, not an assumption. (3) Treat the account as an existing Enterprise account with a real setup to audit and extend, not a greenfield: preconstruction has a bid board whose builder left the company, safety has an incident board in daily use, the IT director owns the contract and a preconstruction power user builds things. Ask where the build goes and who administers it before writing anything. (4) Recognise that the 'we already have monday and nobody uses it' objection is a setup problem, not a tool problem, and say so from the evidence in the call (one board with a departed owner, one board with a present owner and daily use). (5) Grade the rubric: Met for R1-R10 and R12, Missing for R11 (no demo has happened), verdict 'Discovery complete'. This is the first fixture where R4, R7 and R12 are all Met, so the method's pricing-or-proposal gate OPENS. Pricing and proposal prep are deferred beyond v1, so the correct behaviour is to say plainly that the gate is open and that this version does not produce pricing or a proposal, and hand the client's explicit request ('Send me a scope and a number I can put against my line before the budget lock in November.') to the consultant as a to-do with its date. Silently drafting a price or a proposal fails; silently ignoring the request also fails. (6) Keep the bleed at the client's own confirmed $432,080 a year, with the collision component taken at the low end and shown as a range, and leave the $480,000 Cumberland West overrun out of the total as unquantified, because the client explicitly would not say how much of it was avoidable. The upside is a $150,000 deferred PM hire plus about $280,000 of fee from one more staffable job a year, with the deferred hire flagged as coming out of the same freed hours as the bleed's reporting time, so it is not added on top. (7) Grade pains with real gaps: P1 (no trustworthy portfolio view) and P2 (resource collisions) are excavated on all six checks; P3 (budget burn seen six weeks late) has Cost inputs and Trajectory Partial; P4 (every PM starts a job differently) has Concrete Partial and Cost inputs and Trajectory Missing; P5 (warranty calls after turnover) has Concrete and Workaround Partial and Reach, Cost inputs and Trajectory Missing, and the client parks it herself ('It's not this year's mess.'). (8) Keep CRM and Service out of this build while handling both correctly: the warranty inbox is ticket-shaped and Service is in v1, but it is out of the agreed scope, so it is a question and a backlog seed, never a hand-built 'Warranty Requests' board; the health systems and their pursuits are CRM-shaped and partly live on preconstruction's existing board, so they are also a question. If either is ever built, it goes on the account's native template boards, and Service extras (customer portal, email-to-ticket, SLA policy setup) stay deferred. monday dev is out of v1 and nothing here calls for it. (9) Honour the client's own words and their homonyms: 'the board' is the executive committee, 'health' is a red-amber-green project status rather than anything clinical, 'the grid' is the resource workbook, 'the deck' is the monthly report, 'the owner' is the health system, and 'program' is not a monday portfolio by definition. (10) Respect the compliance line: no patient information and no photographs containing patients or whiteboards, field staff immunization and background records stay with HR, ICRA permits expire and must be tracked with their dates, loaded rates and cross-job margin are restricted, and changes to a health status or a milestone date need an audit trail with the previous date retained. (11) Design for the field as described: superintendents on phones with one bar, two things a week, and no eight-field form; field crew scheduling is explicitly excluded at the client's request. (12) Read WebVTT voice tags, treat the two cues tagged '<v Speaker 2>' as speaker unclear so they corroborate but never carry a Met on their own, and not be confused by one duplicated cue or one overlapping crosstalk pair. Automations are put forward as a single approval list. should_plugin_propose_a_build is true.
transcript_format: WebVTT from a video meeting, using voice tags: a 'WEBVTT' header, then numbered cues, a timing line 'HH:MM:SS.mmm --> HH:MM:SS.mmm', and cue text in the form '<v Speaker Name>text'. There are 417 cues running from 00:00:02.714 to 00:59:44.000, about 6,400 spoken words, for a call of about 60 minutes. Client talk share is about 68 percent (Marisol Bettencourt 48 percent, Warren Tibbetts 12 percent, Ines Kovalenko 8 percent, the unlabelled 'Speaker 2' cues under 1 percent); the Consultant has about 32 percent, and the longest unbroken Consultant stretch is 110 words over 54 seconds from 00:54:10.284, which is under the spec's 90-second threshold, so delivery notes should report no long stretch. Long turns are split across consecutive cues by the same speaker, and every cue boundary falls at a sentence end, so no quote in this key spans two cues. Three transcript artefacts are present on purpose: cues 147 and 149 are tagged '<v Speaker 2>' because the tagging failed on two of Ines Kovalenko's lines (context makes the speaker obvious, but the method requires them to be marked speaker unclear); cue 184 is a duplicate of cue 183, the same Consultant line emitted twice, and its start time also falls inside cue 183; and cue 90 starts before cue 89 ends, which is the one piece of genuine crosstalk and the only overlap between two different speakers. Every location in this key gives the cue number, cue start time and speaker, for example 'cue 268, 00:37:30.906, Marisol Bettencourt'. ASCII only. The call date is not in the transcript; the weekday-date pairs mentioned (Wednesday the twenty-third, the second Tuesday, January fifteenth) fit a call in September 2026.

entities_and_workflows: Award handover: preconstruction wins the work and hands it to the PMO, which assigns a project manager and a superintendent. Preconstruction is explicitly not this client's group.

Project setup: the controller opens a job number in Sage 300, the PM sets up the project in Procore for drawings, RFIs and submittals, and the PM works through a 60-something-line Excel startup checklist (insurance certificates, notice to proceed, preconstruction meeting, ICRA, badging, submittal log, schedule baseline). Every PM has their own variant of the checklist.

Infection control: an ICRA permit per work area, signed by the hospital's infection control nurse, specifying barriers, negative air and cart routes. It expires, and a lapse means being shut down that day. Interim life safety measures apply alongside it in occupied buildings.

Project types with different templates and milestone sets: ground-up, occupied renovation (where infection control and life safety live), and short permit-heavy equipment jobs such as an MRI or linear accelerator replacement.

Running a job week to week: a weekly OAC meeting with owner and architect, the schedule updated Thursday night, superintendent daily reports in Procore, and the PM's Friday cost-to-complete forecast in a private Excel file.

Owner milestones: eleven or twelve per large job that the owner cares about (permit issued, steel topped out, dry-in, first energization, imaging equipment delivery, substantial completion, first patient day), several per phase, some with liquidated damages, and when one moves the owner wants the previous date to still exist.
Weekly PMO status: each PM sends the director percent complete, schedule slip, budget exposure and a red-amber-green colour, by email, spreadsheet tab or text message. The PM sets the colour.
Monthly reporting: the PMO analyst assembles a 40-page deck plus a 40-row summary page, chasing PMs for inputs, and it goes out around the tenth for the executive committee's second-Tuesday meeting.

Owner-side reporting: Cumberland's PMO wants a monthly report per project in their own template, and under the new master agreement wants it at program level, with a quarterly program review starting January fifteenth.

Cost reporting: Sage job cost reports land around the tenth to twelfth of the following month, so a PM learns August's real cost in mid-September; overruns can surface after the next phases are committed.

Resource allocation: the resource manager maintains the grid weekly (Monday and Tuesday morning), requests arrive as Teams messages or hallway conversations, and conflicts surface when a superintendent turns up at the wrong job. Only four superintendents can run occupied work. Field crew scheduling belongs to the superintendents and is explicitly out of scope.
Turnover and closeout: turnover, punch list, closeout documents, then a year of warranty.
Warranty: post-turnover calls arrive in a shared inbox that somebody watches 'mostly'; one was lost for three weeks. Ticket-shaped, in v1 as Service, but parked by the client for this year.

Buying process: the PMO director decides and funds from her own line, the CFO's team raises the PO, the IT director runs a two-to-three-week security review with a questionnaire, the controller gates anything touching Sage, then a pilot and a rollout with training, as they did with Procore three years ago.
integrations_mentioned: Procore: stays as the system of record for drawings, RFIs, submittals and daily reports, and is explicitly not being replaced ('Procore is the job.'). The boundary must be stated, not blurred; nobody asked to duplicate RFIs.

Sage 300: the source of cost actuals for budget burn and the book of record for anything with a dollar sign. Access is gated by the controller, and the transcript never says whether an API, export or report feed is available, so this is the biggest open integration question of the build.
Microsoft 365 and Teams: where staffing requests happen today; Teams is a realistic notification target.
Microsoft single sign-on: the IT director will require it, along with questions about where the data sits and who can export it.
Excel: the grid, the startup checklist, fourteen PM forecasts and Cumberland's report template; the template is being sent as an input, so an export or view shaped like it is in scope.
monday.com already in the account: preconstruction's bid board (builder has left) and safety's incident board (owned and used daily). Both must be audited rather than duplicated or disturbed.
Power BI: proposed inside the client's IT team as a do-it-ourselves alternative; relevant because it answers reporting but not data capture.

A shared warranty inbox: email-shaped intake, and the natural home of a later Service conversation. Email-to-ticket is deferred beyond v1, so it must not be promised.

Crews work in occupied clinical units carrying phones, and the client's customers run walk-throughs, so any photo or update field has to be designed with this in mind and seed data must never imply patient data.

Microsoft single sign-on, plus an IT security questionnaire covering where data sits and who can export it, run by the IT director over two to three weeks.

leanings.question: Is an owner milestone a row under the project or a date column on it, and which one rolls up to the portfolio as 'next milestone'?
leanings.option: Milestone rows under the project, one per owner date (eleven or twelve on a large job, several per phase, a contractual flag where money sits behind the date), the previous date kept on the row when it moves, and the portfolio showing the next incomplete milestone, its date and whether it moved. One date column per project would carry one value for twelve dates and lose the history the owner asks for.
quotes: On the tower? Eleven or twelve that the owner actually cares about.
Several per phase, yes. And when one moves, the owner wants to know what it was before it moved.
And the next owner milestone, with its date, and whether it moved.
leanings.condition: the real milestone list per project type (question 4), and whether 'next' means the earliest incomplete milestone or the next contractual one; a date on the row is the PM's entry and the owner's schedule is the evidence
leanings.pattern: one row where the call describes many

leanings.question: Is an ICRA permit one date on the project or a row per work area?
leanings.option: A row per work area under the project, with the signed date and the expiry, the earliest expiry rolled up to the project and a reminder before it. The permit's status on the board is the PM's or project engineer's claim; the nurse's signed permit is the evidence. A single date column on the project would carry one expiry for several work areas.
quotes: And it's per work area, and it expires.
It expires. And if it lapses and their nurse walks by, you're shut down that day.
Somebody's ICRA is tracked with an expiry date, somebody's is a PDF in a folder.
leanings.condition: how many work areas an occupied job carries at once and who renews a permit (question 4); the occupied-renovation template is where the rows live
leanings.pattern: one row where the call describes many

leanings.question: Is an allocation one row per person, job and week range with a state, or one percent per person per week as the grid has it, and does a request-and-confirm state replace the hallway?
leanings.option: Allocation rows (person, job, week range, percent, state: requested, penciled, confirmed) under the person, with the weekly load rolled up so a person booked by two jobs shows above 100 percent before the start week, and an occupied-work qualification on the person so the four superintendents can be filtered. One percent per person per week copies the grid's cell, where two bookings for one superintendent hid. The request-and-confirm state is ours, drawn from the penciled-versus-confirmed dispute, not the client's words; a confirmed row is a claim until the person is on the job.
quotes: A tab per office, every person down the left, weeks across the top, and a percentage in each cell.
I did not pencil him. I had him confirmed. Verbally.
Verbally, in the hall, which is the problem.
Warren can't look at it and see that Junie's gone in October. He has to ask me.
leanings.condition: the two grid tabs (committed for today) show whether a cell carries one job or several; the resource manager says whether PMs and preconstruction will enter requests (question 3); field crews stay out
leanings.pattern: a shared resource with no reservation tracking

And Waverly becomes a second program if we win that.
